title: Power of Four
statement:
Decide whether the integer `n` can be written as `4^x` for some integer exponent `x`. Return `true` if it can and `false` if it cannot. Note that `1 = 4^0` qualifies, while zero and negative numbers never do.

Follow-up: can you answer without any loop or recursion?
notes:
## Intuition

The direct method divides `n` by 4 while it is divisible and checks whether 1 remains, in O(log n) steps. Binary gives a loop-free test. A power of four, `4^x = 2^(2x)`, has exactly one set bit, and that bit sits at an even position: bit 0 for 1, bit 2 for 4, bit 4 for 16, and so on. So two bit checks decide it: exactly one bit set, and that bit is on an even position.

## Approach

1. Zero and negative numbers are never powers of four: return `false`.
2. `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit of `n`; it is `0` exactly when `n` has a single set bit, that is, when `n` is a power of two. If not, return `false`.
3. `evenBitsMask = 0x55555555` is `0101...0101` in binary: every even bit position set. The single bit of `n` is on an even position exactly when `n & evenBitsMask` is non-zero; return that.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 16` is `10000` in binary, so it is positive. `n - 1 = 15` is `01111`, and `16 & 15 = 0`, so `isPowerOfTwo` is `true`. The set bit is bit 4, an even position, so `16 & 0x55555555 = 16`, which is non-zero, and the answer is `true`. For `n = 8` (`1000`, bit 3) the same steps would give `8 & 0x55555555 = 0`, so `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1): a fixed number of bit operations.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Check `n <= 0` first: `0 & -1` is `0`, so zero would pass the power-of-two test.
- Being a power of two is not enough: `2`, `8` and `2^29` have their bit at an odd position.
- The mask test alone is not enough either: `5` is `101`, with both bits at even positions, so the single-bit check must come first.
- Write `(n & (n - 1)) === 0` with parentheses: `&` binds more loosely than `===`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | the number being tested |
| `isPowerOfTwo` | whether `n` has exactly one set bit |
| `evenBitsMask` | `0x55555555`, every even bit position set to 1 |

narration.2: Zero and negative numbers can never equal a power of four.
narration.3: Reject them before looking at the bits.
narration.5: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, leaving 0 only when n has exactly one set bit.
narration.6: More than one set bit means n is not even a power of two...
narration.7: ...so it cannot be a power of four.
narration.9: 0x55555555 has a 1 at every even bit position: 0, 2, 4, ..., 30.
narration.10: The single set bit of n is a power of four exactly when it lands on one of those even positions.
